--- title: "Resgo: Portfolio Simulation" subtitle: "End to end strategic value quantification" author: "Nicholas Dorsch" date: today categories: [LDI, geology, geophysics, statistics] image: media/resgo_logo_white.svg execute: echo: false cache: true --- Resgo still has no UI, but before I start developing it I have one more feature to build: Portfolio simulation. Portfolio simulation is the Resgo end-game. Resgo already provides a very performant Prospect level simulation engine, from subsurface through to commercial metrics, and that leaves it well positioned for zooming out one more level to portfolio level analysis. My goals at the outset are the following: 1. Allow grouping Prospects into Portfolios, with lossless representation 2. Represent parent-child relationships between Prospects to allow for dependency propagation 3. Dependency propagation should allows information to flow between prospects and their children, so that drilling outcomes follow logical chains during simulation 4. Use those logical chains to derive stand-alone and full-cycle metrics for decision gating 5. Report accepted, strategic (full cycle economics says drill) and rejected prospect decisions at the portfolio level 6. Make results interpretable with well designed visualizations ## Structure and constraints The most convenient representation of a Portfolio with these constraints in mind is a tree. Prospects can have children: opportunities who's risks are affected by outcomes in their parent. That creates some limitations (sibling Prospects can't have dependencies) but I think the simplicity of tree depth traversal, and limiting onerous dependency configuration, will make that trade-off worthwhile. For lossless Prospect representation in Resgo, dependency must be represented at the reservoir and risk factor level. This is a complication that I believe will pay dividends in granular configuration and interpretability of portfolio simulations, matching the mental models in subsurface teams' heads when defining dependencies between opportunitities. It will mean, for example, that reservoirs in the Propects tree can share strong P(Charge) dependency. If the parent fails on charge, that heavily impacts the P(Charge) of children. This is well suited for modelling play-openers on untested migration pathways, for example. Similarly these dependencies can be captured for reservoir presence for testing sand fairways, and seal/trap for things like demonstrating fault seal. ## Dependency mechanics I'm going to bring up Bayes again, sorry[^not-sorry]. Dependency in this framing is a Bayesian probability update from the prior risk probability (say a 0.5 probability of charge in the child reservoir). Mechanically, the update is applied in odds space: $$ O_{\mathrm{post}} = O_{\mathrm{prior}} \times \text{LH} $$ or, equivalently, in log-odds space: $$ \ln_2\left(O_{\mathrm{post}}\right) = \ln_2\left(O_{\mathrm{prior}}\right) + \ln_2\left(\text{LH}\right) $$ where $O = p / (1 - p)$ is the odds, $\text{LH}$ is the likelihood ratio, and $\ln_2$ denotes a base-2 logarithm. Using a base-2 logarithm means that the evidence term, $\ln_2(\text{LH})$, is measured in **bits**: positive bits increase the odds of success, negative bits decrease them, and zero bits leave the prior odds unchanged. You'll have to humor me---I know it seems weird---but this is a very mentally ergonomic way of framing Bayesian probability updates. Starting from a prior probability of 0.50 as an example, each additional bit doubles the likelihood ratio: | Evidence | Likelihood ratio | Posterior probability | |---:|---:|---:| | -4 bits | 1:16 | 0.06 | | -3 bits | 1:8 | 0.11 | | -2 bits | 1:4 | 0.20 | | -1 bit | 1:2 | 0.33 | | 0 bits | 1:1 | 0.50 | | 1 bit | 2:1 | 0.67 | | 2 bits | 4:1 | 0.80 | | 3 bits | 8:1 | 0.89 | | 4 bits | 16:1 | 0.94 | Operating in this way means that updates are commutative: you can add and subtract bits of evidence to arrive at a final posterior. This is mental Bayes trickery, but is also useful for efficient and interpretable communication of risk dependencies in the context of the portfolio simulator. > _"If the Buffet prospect fails on charge, how bad would that be for charge risk at > Bonanza?"_ > > _"They're on the same migration corridor so really bad... probably -4 bits."_ > > _"We did see shows on that separate migration corridor connecting to Bonanza though, > remember?"_ > > _"Fair enough, that's probably worth 1 bit. -3 bits total then."_ Now, regardless of P(Charge) at Buffet, the information it provides to Bonanza is explicitly communicated. If, for example, P(Charge) is 0.5 across prospects and Buffet fails on charge, that means Bonanza gets a P(Charge) of 0.11 (killing it). If Buffet _is_ charged though, that increase P(Charge) at Bonanza to 0.89! See? We can all become Bayesians with some language tricks. There is a technical wrinkle that positive and negative updates are not necessarily symmetric (relevant example [here](https://nick-dorsch.github.io/blog/posts/confusion/)), so the code should make that explicit, but default to symmetric updates. ## Decision Gates For the portfolio simulation to be coherent, decisions need to be made about whether to drill for each Prospect, based on the information available. That requires point estimate hurdles. Decisions aren't made stochastically. We can't just use the simulation result to determine the right path on every iteration, because the decision maker doesn't know what will happen. That means a decision criterion needs to be specified. This can be things like a positive risked mean NPV (equivalent to EMV): $$ \mathbb{E}\left[\mathrm{NPV}_{\mathrm{risked}}\right] > 0 $$ or a positive risked 90th percentile NPV: $$ Q_{0.10}\left(\mathrm{NPV}_{\mathrm{risked}}\right) > 0 $$ But it needs to be agreed upon up front for the portfolio simulation to operate. Most companies have defined hurdles like this in place, but there may be situations where hurdles are prospect specific. Luckily, because Resgo simulates everything in a single integrated chain, these decision metrics will be consistently applied to rigorously defined stochastic ranges of NPV. I would imagine that that is a rare luxury in portfolio analysis contexts. ## Simulation process Resgo allows us to very ergonomically simulate the entire portfolio tree in a forward pass, adjusting risk factors on success/failure case of parent nodes, then run the decision gating logic on the results to determine which prospects get drilled and which get rejected. We can then aggregate the portfolio level NPV to assess its overall economic value and uncertainty. ## Additional wrinkles Because we are simulating an ensemble of prospects, we need to be careful to define a few things up front. We need a single price deck, especially if it is stochastic, to avoid individual prospects getting their own price histories. We also need a single economic basis for escalation and discounting. That means every prospect has NPV calculations consistent on a single "start date" for the whole portfolio. Failing to do this would unfairly inflate the value of future prospects in the schedule. ## Strategic value Something compelling that this gives us is the ability to quantify the strategic value of prospects. This is the stand-alone value of the prospect, plus any downstream opportunity it creates. This means that a stand-alone prospect with negative NPV---maybe due to a low P(Success)---can have its downstream value quantified and summed to make it _full-cycle_ economic, even if it is not drillable on its own merits. For example: ```{mermaid} flowchart TD Buffet["Buffet
P(Success): 0.45
NPV: $180MM"] Buffet --> Cove["Cove
P(Success): 0.35
NPV: $70MM"] Buffet --> Ledge["Ledge
P(Success): 0.55
NPV: $75MM"] Buffet --> Bridge["Bridge
P(Success): 0.10
NPV: -$200MM"] Bridge --> Bonanza["Bonanza
P(Success): 0.15
NPV: $1,200MM"] Bonanza --> Crest["Crest
P(Success): 0.20
NPV: $700MM"] Bonanza --> Saddle["Saddle
P(Success): 0.18
NPV: $650MM"] Bonanza --> Spur["Spur
P(Success): 0.12
NPV: $1,000MM"] ``` Hear me out. Bridge is a high risk, low return prospect. It will probably fail, and it's a small closure. It's a dog. But if Buffet were successful, you'd be crazy not to drill Bridge next. This is the crazy senior geologist speaking. He has a mad twinkle in his eye, and he knows nobody will listen, but he knows he is _right, dammit_. Why is he right? Because the information that Bridge provides, expensive as it may be, has huge upside. A success at Bridge would boost the P(Success) of Bonanza, a high risk, high reward prospect that nobody is considering because "there is no migration that way". Bonanza is a _play opener_, it has several follow-ups, all of which are currently high risk, but high value. So you drill Bridge to open up the play. I've been the crazy guy before. I've never been able to quantify any of this stuff persuasively. Resgo lets me quantify the whole lot, all the way through to economics. It all flows naturally as a consequence of your decision metrics, and the risks and uncertainties in your portfolio. Resgo tells you to do it. And the tool isn't crazy! It's just uncertainty propagation, Bayesian updating and commercial modelling. Don't argue with the results, just make sure you verify your inputs. Now let's try to do it. # Example Here's the Portfolio tree again, without risks and NPVs as we haven't calculated them yet: ```{mermaid} flowchart TD Buffet[Buffet] Buffet --> Cove[Cove] Buffet --> Ledge[Ledge] Buffet --> Bridge[Bridge] Bridge --> Bonanza[Bonanza] Bonanza --> Crest[Crest] Bonanza --> Saddle[Saddle] Bonanza --> Spur[Spur] ``` My goal with this example will be to live demo the sequence I spelled out in the previous section on strategic value. This is all make believe, but what I want to try and illustrate is that standalone prospect economics is insufficient for good opportunity ranking or decision making. These prospects will look far too risky to drill on their own, but at a portfolio level warrant serious consideration. First, let's define these prospects. All prospects will share the same set of reservoir targets, named "Archer", "Boulder", "Canyon" and "Drift". This will be a bit of a repetitive section, so feel free to look through one prospect, then skip ahead. ## Prospects ### Buffet Buffet is a risky but high upside prospect that is the overall play opener for the portfolio. The biggest concern the team has is with charge, as they are not convinced a migration pathway exists at this location. The trap size is also a big uncertainty, leading to wide uncertainty in outcomes. #### Volumetrics ::: {#53e03fdc .cell execution_count=6} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=128} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## High risk You'll notice this entire portfolio is very high risk. That is because all risk factors are being applied with our current state of information. The entire portfolio has high charge risk, a P(Charge) of 0.4 for Buffet, Cove, Ledge and Bridge, and an even harsher 0.1 for Bonanza and its children, making them all a bad bet. This is an untested migration corridor in our exploration acreage. The opportunities don't necessarily hold up on their own merits. Buffet, the entire play opener, is negative EMV! That is why strategic value is so important. Strategic, full-cycle value of these prospects will be simulated on a portfolio basis, and that will provide us with a richer picture of value. ## Portfolio model The portfolio manages all these prospects, along with their parent-child relationships and information sharing for risk factors. For simplicity we will just model information sharing for P(Charge), but a user could model relationships between reservoir risk factors as they see fit. ### Charge dependency The charge dependency between reservoir intersections is intuitive. Information we acquire on a migration corridor (observing charged) changes the risk factors applied to any child prospects in the portfolio. In this example we give charge +3 bits of information. So if Buffet fails on charge, the whole portfolio dies, but if it succeeds, the portfolio lights up like a christmas tree, and we follow the opportunity branches. Importantly, the information flowing is not contingent on _commercial_ success, it is contingent on the observation regarding that particular risk factor. If Buffet is charged, but tiny and sub economic, that doesn't change anything for the child prospects, what matters is that Buffet is charged! ### Visualizing results The Resgo Portfolio, as it turns out, is quite a complicated object to visualize. Bifurcation also effectively means very high NPV vs almost certain failure, given how sensitive we are to charge risk. That creates very wide uncertainties. Neat! ## Overall thoughts Okay, so there is a lot to unpack here. The first thing that jumps out at me is that the commercial outcomes at the portfolio aggregated level are incredibly uncertain. This isn't surprising, if you think about it. We don't even know if this corridor is charged. That means we have anything between zero value here, and potentially 8 decently sized prospects. That is going to be a very wide range. Furthermore, at each level in the tree we have risk bifurcation, which means prospect outcomes get split into two paths. This further widens portfolio level uncertainty. To illustrate this a bit more: If Buffet fails, the entire portfolio is ruled out. Too risky on charge. If Buffet succeeds, that boosts the P(Charge) of its children Cove, Ledge, and Bridge. That doesn't mean they all succeed (other risk factors are at play) but they become much more likely to. If Bridge is charged, that information flows to Bonanza and its children. These prospects were written off as extremely high risk before drilling with P(Charge) of 0.1. The success upstream at Bridge, even though Bridge on its own is sub-economic, opens up the Bonanza play. That has huge strategic value, as Bonanza is the biggest prospect in the portfolio on an unrisked basis. Because of the dependencies between prospects in the portfolio, standalone economic metrics aren't enough to capture opportunity value. Most of the value in Buffet is not standalone, it is in the downstream information it provides to child prospects, connected via the P(Charge) dependency. Similarly, Bridge would never get drilled on its own merits---it would disappear in the rankings of a naive opportunity register---it provides value via its downstream consequences. These complicated arguments are _very_ difficult to make in normal circumstances, especially under uncertainty. This is my best attempt at making the whole simulated system explicit. ## A note on means and medians Something else this exercise has clarified for me, is that summary statistics like the mean and median are horribly reductive when uncertainties are this wide. The whole point of drilling Buffet and opening up this play is the _exposure to upside_. On a mean (expected) basis, the decision is supported because the portfolio is NPV positive... but that isn't the real reason for doing it. According to the model there is a 10% chance this portfolio is worth more than $2.7 billion dollars in net present value. The mean is $580 million. The range is really important to keep in mind, because we aren't going to discover the mean portfolio outcome, we're going to be strapped onto an uncertainty rocket with no way of knowing where we end up. Considering the downside exposure vs upside exposure is more informative than an abstract mean that will never happen. In the previous post on Resgo prospect simulation, I brought up loss functions, and I think they are even more relevant at this level of analysis. As for the median... throw it out. It is very misleading because the outcome NPV distributions we are considering are so long tailed. It just doesn't make sense as a metric if you take uncertainty seriously. So the mean is lossy, but the median is not representative. ## Portfolio optimization I haven't built it yet (maybe it'll be the topic of my next post on Resgo), but this simulation chain also creates a very powerful optimization surface. A discrete optimization model---shifting prospect drill order, wells per prospect, delays---under capital allocation and infrastructure constraints, where the target is discounted cash flows (so the benefit of acting sooner is implicit in the optimization), is... very nice. ## Where is the D-Tree? This whole simulation can be thought of as a stochastic D-Tree, with Bayesian updates informing success/failure at each node, and full cycle economics driving drill/walk decisions. I don't have a pretty plot presenting it that way, but mechanically, that is what this it is doing. # Closing thoughts I'm not sure how to close this out, but I will say that I am very happy with how portfolio simulation in Resgo has turned out. I've always had it as a "capstone" feature in the back of my mind, but I can't claim that I designed for it from the beginning. I was fortunately very lucky that the implementation fit so well into Resgo's architecture. Treating Prospects as nodes in a tree, and simply simulating that tree with a few in loop alterations based on risk dependencies, is a pretty elegant way of handling portfolio analysis. The part I am now unsure about is how to rigorously define all these metrics. Reporting quantities like Standalone Success NPV, Full Cycle Success NPV, portfolio aggregated NPV, and whatever other commercial metrics I will add later, start to build up and cause confusion. Handling geological success as a commercial outcome (ie an NPV negative dry hole) changes the semantics of prospect evaluation, because traditionally the failure case would be captured as a failure arm in a D-Tree. That isn't the elegant approach here, I can go a lot further by naturally capturing a range in a single simulated array, and reasoning about it downstream, but there are definitely some semantic rough edges to figure out. My next step I think will be to start building a UI---refining the simulation code itself is probably the most important thing to be focussed on---but I also need to be able to get Resgo into other people's hands at some point, barring me using it in a consultancy capacity only. I do like the consultancy approach, at least at first, because it will allow me to field test with real opportunities, and iron out any creases I've left in the process.
